summary:
Swaroop Chitlur Haridas and Nachiket Paranjape from DoorDash's horizontal GenAI Platform team walk through how eval expanded from an internal engineering concern into a cross-functional discipline at DoorDash. The platform serves every product team and helps them balance three forces — accuracy, latency, and cost — across models and agents. Primitives include an LLM gateway, an agent gateway that centralizes authentication and agent identity for security, and open-weights model hosting that has already delivered cost wins.

Initial customer conversations exposed very different eval needs: consumer discovery needed session-level judgments, personalization ML needed scaled human judgment, and multi-agent systems needed trajectory-based eval. Rather than build bespoke UIs for each, the team took guidance from co-founder Andy Fang and became UI-first for non-engineers, then API-first so engineers could build independently, and now workflow-first so PMs and strat-ops can operate the platform themselves using coding agents.

Evals are explicitly framed as a team sport. Strategy and ops set priorities and the quality bar; product managers translate requirements into rubrics and workflows; operations runs annotation; engineering owns APIs, telemetry, datasets, and judges. The continuous loop is: capture traces and sessions, sample down to a reviewable set, annotate with domain expertise, promote golden datasets, calibrate LLM judges, monitor, and repeat.

The platform exposes two surfaces: a telemetry layer for traces and scores accessible via MCP, SDK, and APIs, and a workflow surface where strat-ops and PMs run annotations, review golden sets, and create and calibrate judges. Because every surface is API-first, strat-ops teams use tools like Cursor or Claude Code to vibe-code bespoke annotation UIs — for example, grading restaurant menus or annotating images. Judge calibration is self-serve through a UI built on the DSPy library; PMs set configs, run optimization loops across Claude, OpenAI, or Gemini, and see original versus optimized prompts side-by-side to build trust. Prompt ownership legitimately varies across teams — strategy/ops, PMs, or engineering — and the platform treats that variation as healthy organizational learning rather than a problem to standardize. The closing remarks highlight that this self-serve approach reduced per-annotation spend at DoorDash scale (thousands of rows weekly), accelerated iteration, and enabled teams to calibrate judges fully on their own.

sections.title: Opening and the GenAI Platform Team's three forces
sections.summary: Swaroop and Nachiket introduce themselves as part of DoorDash's horizontal GenAI Platform team that helps product teams balance accuracy, latency, and cost across models and agents. Primitives include an LLM gateway, an agent gateway handling auth and agent identity, and open-weights model hosting that has already delivered cost wins. Eval is positioned as the team's fourth pillar.

sections.title: Why eval became the fourth pillar
sections.summary: Conversations with internal product teams surfaced very different needs: session-level quality judgments for consumer discovery, scaled human judgment for personalization, and trajectory-based eval for multi-agent systems. Rather than build a UI per use case, the team followed co-founder Andy Fang's guidance to be UI-first for non-engineers, then API-first so engineers are not blocked, and now workflow-first so PMs and strat-ops can run operations themselves using coding agents.

sections.title: Evals as a team sport, not an engineering harness
sections.summary: Nachiket reframes evals as a cross-functional effort. Strategy and ops set priorities and quality bars, PMs translate requirements into rubrics and workflows, ops runs annotations, and engineering supplies APIs, telemetry, datasets, and judges. The continuous iteration loop is: trace, sample down to a reviewable set, annotate with domain expertise, build golden datasets, calibrate judges, monitor, and repeat.

sections.title: Two surfaces: telemetry and workflow
sections.summary: The platform exposes a telemetry layer holding traces, scores, and observations, accessible via MCP, SDK, and APIs. The workflow surface is where strat-ops, PMs, and ops set annotation tasks, review golden datasets, and create and calibrate judges. Both are powered by stable APIs the platform team owns.

sections.title: Operators vibe-coding their own annotation UIs
sections.summary: Because the team is API-first, strat-ops partners use tools like Cursor and Claude Code to vibe-code annotation UIs for their own use cases — for example, grading a restaurant menu or annotating images. The platform team does not need to anticipate every UI; operators build what they need against the same endpoints.

sections.title: Self-serve judge calibration UI
sections.summary: Judge calibration is exposed as a self-serve UI built on the DSPy library. PMs and operators set configs, run optimization loops using Claude, OpenAI, or Gemini, and elevate calibrated prompts as their LLM-as-a-judge. A side-by-side view of the original and optimized system prompt builds trust, and the team highlights a case where calibration produced significant improvement.

sections.title: Different teams, different prompt owners
sections.summary: Swaroop notes that prompt ownership legitimately varies across teams — strategy/ops, product managers, or engineering can each own the judge prompt in different configurations. The platform treats that variation as healthy organizational learning, gives teams flexibility to design and evolve their own setup, and emphasizes self-serve operation so teams are not blocked on the platform team.

sections.title: Quality loop in practice and annotation cost reduction
sections.summary: Nachiket recaps the self-serve philosophy and concrete outcomes: reusing DoorDash's existing infrastructure, the platform moved UI-first to API-first to workflow-first and saw a sharp reduction in per-annotation spend despite annotating thousands of rows weekly. Faster loops let teams iterate, calibrate judges self-serve, and move at very high velocity.

sections.title: Closing: the eight-step continuous loop
sections.summary: Nachiket revisits the eight-step continuous loop slide — traces, sessions, sampling, annotation with human and domain knowledge, golden datasets, calibrating workflows, agents, and LLM judges, then repeating — as the team's repeatable recipe for shipping reliably with high quality. The talk closes with applause and an offer to take questions.
